**The Corner Above the Window**

Fennimore was born in the gap behind Delia's bathroom mirror, and he fell in love with her on his third day of life, when she sang "I Wanna Dance with Somebody" off-key into a hairbrush at seven in the morning.

He decided to introduce himself properly. He spun his finest dragline, lowered himself from the ceiling until he hung level with her face, and raised two front legs in what he hoped was a friendly wave.

Delia screamed so loudly that the neighbor's dog started barking. She threw a slipper. It missed, but barely, and Fennimore spent the next two days trembling behind the towel rack, absorbing the hardest lesson of his short life: Delia loved a great many things, and none of them had eight legs.

So he decided to love her from a distance.

He worked at night. When mosquitoes drifted through the cracked window and whined around her ears, he caught them. When fruit flies swarmed the bananas on her counter, they vanished one by one. A moth that had been chewing holes in her favorite green sweater met a quiet end in the back of the closet. Every morning, Fennimore took down his webs before she woke, so she would never have to see them.

"It's so weird," Delia told her sister on the phone in August. "I haven't had a single bug bite all summer."

Listening from the shadows, Fennimore felt almost unbearably proud.

Then, one night in September, Delia couldn't sleep. She switched on the lamp just as Fennimore was wrapping up a fat mosquito six inches above her pillow.

They stared at each other.

He waited for the slipper. Her hands were shaking. She reached slowly toward the nightstand, and he braced himself, but instead of a weapon, she picked up her glasses.

"Was that you?" she whispered. "All summer?"

He didn't know how to answer, so he held perfectly still, which is what spiders do instead of nodding.

Delia took a long, unsteady breath. "Okay," she said finally. "Okay. You can have the corner above the window. But you stay up there. If you ever touch me, I'm moving out."

It wasn't the kind of love anyone writes songs about. But Fennimore took the corner.

And every morning after that, without ever quite looking up, Delia said, "Morning, Steve."

His name wasn't Steve. He didn't mind at all. For a spider, that was practically a wedding.

# Asia's Richest Man Builds a $193 Million Monastery — Complete With Bulletproof VIP Rooms

HONG KONG — A lavish Buddhist monastery financed by Li Ka-shing, Asia's richest man, will open to the public by mid-April, offering visitors a close-up view of one of the largest statues of the Goddess of Mercy ever built — and, for a privileged few, rooms protected by bulletproof glass.

Tsz Shan Monastery, whose name translates roughly as "Mountain of Compassion," sits on a green hillside in Tai Po, in Hong Kong's New Territories. The complex cost about HK$1.5 billion, or $193 million, and was paid for through the tycoon's charitable foundation after years of planning and construction.

Towering over the grounds is a gleaming white bronze statue of Guan Yin, the bodhisattva of compassion revered across East Asia. At 76 meters (about 250 feet), it is believed to be the second-tallest Guan Yin statue in the world, surpassed only by a 108-meter figure in Sanya, on China's southern island province of Hainan.

The monastery's more worldly touches have drawn just as much attention. Its VIP rooms are reported to be fitted with bulletproof windows, a feature more often associated with embassies than with places of meditation. The precaution may reflect the high-profile guests the monastery expects to receive, as well as the security concerns that come with being tied to one of the world's wealthiest men.

Li, 86, built an empire spanning ports, property, telecommunications and retail, and his fortune is estimated at more than $30 billion. He is also one of Hong Kong's most prominent philanthropists and has famously described his foundation as his "third son," pledging a third of his assets to it.

Visitors won't pay to get in, but they won't be able to simply turn up, either. Entry will be handled through an online booking system, with daily numbers capped to keep the grounds peaceful. Organizers have said they want Tsz Shan to remain a place for reflection and the study of Buddhism rather than another stop on the city's crowded tourist circuit.

That would set it apart from Hong Kong's best-known Buddhist landmark, the 34-meter Tian Tan Buddha on Lantau Island, which draws busloads of sightseers every day.

Whether a monastery with a 76-meter goddess and bulletproof glass can stay off the tourist map remains to be seen. For now, anyone hoping to see Guan Yin up close will need to book ahead.

Dr. Albers says I should write you a letter I'm not going to send. She says it will help me "process." So: hi, Theo. Let's process.

You changed your number again. That's fine. I'm not upset. I know how you get when you're overwhelmed: you shut down, you push people away, you buy a new SIM card at the pharmacy on Fourth Street at 8:42 on a Tuesday night. I'm not judging. It's one of the things I love about you. You've always been a little dramatic.

Let me clear something up about the key, since your sister made such a scene. You gave it to me. Willingly. On a little keychain shaped like an avocado, because I was "the good half." You never asked for it back, so when I let myself in on Wednesdays, I wasn't breaking in. I was visiting. I watered the fern you always forget. I put the mugs back in the cabinet by the stove, where they belong, where they have always belonged. I took one sock. Just one. You never noticed. Once I left a lasagna. You threw it away. I checked.

You changed the locks after that, which, honestly, felt like an overreaction to lasagna.

Then there's Priya.

I'll admit I've spent some time on Priya. Her Instagram is public, which says a lot about a person. Four hundred and twelve posts. I've seen all of them, most of them more than once. She does hot yoga. She uses the word "grateful" an alarming amount. In March she went to Lisbon with her sisters and wore a hat that, Theo, I'm sorry, did not work.

You look happy in the ones she tags you in. But I know that smile. That's your polite smile. That's the smile you used to give my mother.

The restraining order came on a Friday. Your lawyer is very thorough. I read it four times, and now I keep it in my nightstand. Do you realize it's the first official document with both our names on it? Not the lease, because you "weren't ready." Not a wedding invitation, because we never got that far. But this. Petitioner. Respondent. Side by side, like a dedication in a book.

Five hundred feet. I measured. The bench across from your building is five hundred and nine. I'm not unreasonable. Some mornings I sit there with my coffee, completely within the law, and if you happened to look out your window, you'd see that I'm doing very well. I've started wearing my hair differently.

But the bench isn't the point anymore. I'm telling you all this because I've found a way to make everything easier for all of us.

I joined a hot yoga studio. The one on Delancey, Tuesdays and Thursdays at six. I go by Jess there. It's my middle name, so it isn't even a lie. Priya is so much warmer in person than she is online. She thinks I'm a dental hygienist from Queens. We get smoothies after class. Last week she told me her boyfriend's ex was "a lot," and that she's been "holding space" for him while he heals. I said that sounded really hard. I squeezed her hand.

She's invited me to her birthday dinner next month. She says she can't wait for me to meet you.

I can't either.

Dr. Albers says I shouldn't send this letter, and I won't. I'll just bring it with me. You can read it at the table.

I'll wear green. You always liked me in green.

The use of animals in scientific research is one of the most difficult ethical questions in modern science. Supporters point out that animal studies have contributed to nearly every major medical advance, from vaccines to cancer treatments, and that many questions about whole living systems cannot yet be answered with cell cultures or computer models. Without such research, human suffering would likely increase.

Critics respond that animals can feel pain and fear, and that their suffering is not justified simply because it benefits another species. They also note that results in animals do not always translate to humans.

A reasonable position lies between the extremes. Animal research can be ethical when it is truly necessary, when no alternative exists, and when suffering is minimized. The widely accepted "Three Rs" framework, Replacement, Reduction and Refinement, captures this approach. Society should continue to invest in alternatives so that, over time, fewer animals are needed at all.

In role-playing games like Dungeons & Dragons, and in many MMOs, the cleric is the classic support character. Groups bring one along because clerics cover jobs that are hard to fill any other way.

**Why parties want a cleric**

- **Healing.** Clerics restore hit points during and after combat, letting fighters and other front-liners survive longer fights.
- **Recovery from disaster.** They can cure poison, disease, and curses, and at higher levels even bring dead characters back to life.
- **Buffs and protection.** Spells like Bless or Shield of Faith make the whole team more accurate and harder to hit.
- **Handling undead.** Clerics can turn or destroy undead creatures, which makes certain dungeons far less dangerous.
- **Flexibility.** Many clerics wear solid armor and can hold their own in melee, so they aren't just hiding at the back.

**What happens without one**

A party can absolutely survive without a cleric, but it has to adapt:

- The group leans on healing potions, which cost gold and run out.
- Characters need to rest more often, which can give enemies time to regroup or let a time-sensitive quest slip away.
- Other classes, such as druids, bards, or paladins, may step in as part-time healers.
- Characters die more often, and a death may be permanent if nobody can cast revival magic.
- Players tend to fight more cautiously, skip risky encounters, and rely more on stealth or diplomacy.

In most modern games a cleric isn't strictly required, but it works as a safety net. Without that net, every mistake hurts more, which some groups actually enjoy as an extra challenge.

Radiation forces and torques exerted by acoustic fields on small particles underpin a wide range of acoustofluidic, levitation, and particle-manipulation technologies, yet their connection to fundamental field properties has remained incompletely understood. In this work, we derive general expressions for the acoustic radiation force and torque acting on small (Rayleigh) particles in arbitrary monochromatic sound fields, accounting for both the monopole and dipole responses of the particle. We show that the non-gradient, radiation-pressure component of the force is directly proportional to the canonical momentum density of the acoustic wave, whereas the radiation torque is determined by the spin angular momentum density associated with the local elliptical motion of the medium's velocity field. These results establish a close analogy with optical forces and torques on dipolar particles and provide a physically transparent interpretation of acoustic momentum and spin. Furthermore, they indicate that small probe particles can serve as direct local measures of these otherwise elusive dynamical quantities, with implications for structured acoustic fields and acoustic manipulation.

**DEEPLY SORRY**

*Genre:* Comedy
*Starring:* Jim Carrey
*Tone:* *Liar Liar* meets *The Mask*, with the heart of *The Truman Show*

---

**Logline**

The world's most successful professional apologizer, a man paid to take the blame for the rich and famous, discovers he has never sincerely apologized for anything in his life. He has one week to learn how before he loses the only person who ever believed in him.

---

**Synopsis**

**Walt Fennimore** (Jim Carrey) has a gift: nobody says "I'm sorry" like Walt. He can weep on cue, collapse to his knees in heartbreaking contrition, and deliver a tearful public statement so moving that people forget what the scandal was about.

Ten years ago Walt was a failed regional theater actor. Then he took a temp job reading a politician's apology at a press conference, and the clip went viral. Now he runs **Mea Culpa Inc.**, a boutique agency that rents him out to celebrities, CEOs and influencers. When a pop star insults a whole country, Walt flies in as her "personal spiritual advisor" and takes the blame for "writing the tweet." When a tech billionaire's self-driving lawnmower terrorizes a retirement community, Walt plays the "rogue engineer" who reprogrammed it. He has been fired, publicly shamed, and dramatically escorted out of buildings more than four hundred times. He has a loyalty card at the paparazzi's favorite coffee shop.

Walt is rich, loud and completely shameless. He's also lonely, though he would never admit it.

The only person who sees through him is his ex-wife, **Nora** (a warm, grounded role suited to someone like Rachel McAdams). She's a public school music teacher, and their 12-year-old daughter **Pip** has inherited Walt's flair for drama. Walt misses Pip's recitals, forgets birthdays and covers every failure with a dazzling, theatrical apology that means nothing. Nora has had enough. She's moving with Pip to Toronto at the end of the week.

---

**The Hook**

Walt lands the biggest client of his career. **Chase Dunmore** (a smug, scene-stealing villain role) is a tech mogul whose company caused a citywide blackout. Chase pays Walt seven figures to pose as the employee responsible. There's a catch: Pip's school orchestra was performing at the concert hall that lost power, and Pip was trapped in an elevator for three hours. Walt can't take the blame for hurting his own daughter.

Then something strange happens. After a run-in with a mysterious elderly janitor at the concert hall (a small, magical cameo), Walt finds he **physically cannot apologize** for anything he didn't do. Each time he tries to fake one, his body revolts. His face twists into grotesque grimaces, his limbs lock into contortions, and his voice cracks into gibberish. On live television, he attempts Chase's apology and ends up doing an involuntary interpretive dance across the press-room table.

This is the core comedic engine. It gives Carrey a reason to deliver the elastic, all-out physical comedy that made *Ace Ventura* and *Liar Liar* iconic, while the emotional stakes keep it grounded.

---

**Act Two**

His business collapses. Every celebrity client he's ever covered for comes out of the woodwork, demanding he "fix" their new scandals. Chase hires a cutthroat replacement apologizer and starts a smear campaign to make Walt the scapegoat for the blackout anyway.

Desperate, Walt realizes the curse only lets him apologize for things he actually did. He sets out to make **real** apologies to the people he has wronged: Nora, Pip, his estranged brother, a former theater castmate whose big break he stole, and a coffee shop barista he has tipped exactly one cent since 2014. Each apology is harder and funnier than the last, because Walt has no idea how to be sincere without performing. In one standout sequence, he has to apologize to a children's birthday party he once ruined while dressed as a hot dog, and he does it while dressed as a hot dog.

Slowly, the man who could fake any emotion starts feeling real ones.

---

**Act Three**

With Nora's move one day away and Chase on the verge of escaping justice, Walt uses his skills one last time. This time he uses them for the truth. He crashes Chase's televised "Corporate Responsibility Summit" and stages an elaborate, chaotic performance. It tricks Chase into publicly confessing, then leaves the billionaire twitching uncontrollably when he tries to fake his own apology. It turns out the curse is contagious.

Walt rushes to Pip's rescheduled recital, misses the start, and slips in quietly at the back. Then he does the most radical thing of his life. He doesn't make a scene. He just watches and listens.

Afterward, he gives Nora and Pip a short, simple, unrehearsed apology. Nora doesn't take him back right away, but she postpones the move. In the final scene, Walt opens a new business called **Sorry School**, where he teaches people how to apologize sincerely. On day one, his only student is Chase Dunmore.

---

**Why It Works for Carrey**

*Deeply Sorry* gives Carrey a hero who is a nonstop human cartoon on the outside and a broken man underneath, which is the exact mix behind his biggest hits. It is high-concept, endlessly quotable and full of physical set pieces built for trailers. It is also a comedy about public shame and accountability in the internet age. That timeliness would make it feel fresh rather than nostalgic, and could put Carrey back where he belongs: at the center of a crowd-pleasing summer comedy.

A U.S. military official said Wednesday that the fall of the Iraqi city of Ramadi to ISIS militants is "not imminent," even as a local official inside the city warned that government forces may not be able to hold out much longer.

Ramadi, the capital of Anbar province, lies about 110 kilometers (70 miles) west of Baghdad and has been contested for more than a year. In recent days, ISIS fighters have pushed into neighborhoods on the city's eastern edge, forcing thousands of residents to flee toward the capital.

Speaking to CNN, the U.S. official acknowledged the situation was serious but said Iraqi security forces still controlled key government buildings in the city center and continued to receive coalition air support.

An official in Ramadi offered a far bleaker assessment. He said it was unclear how long the city's defenders, many of them police officers and local tribal fighters, could continue to resist without fresh troops, weapons and supplies. He pleaded with the Iraqi government in Baghdad to send reinforcements immediately and urged the U.S.-led coalition to step up airstrikes on militant positions around the city.

The loss of Ramadi would be a major setback for Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi's government, which recaptured Tikrit only weeks ago and has vowed that Anbar will be the next front in the campaign against ISIS.

The coalition said it has conducted several strikes near Ramadi in recent days and is monitoring the situation closely.

Medieval townspeople relied on a combination of natural sources and, increasingly, public infrastructure.

The most common source was the well, whether privately owned, shared among neighbors, or maintained by the town. Rivers and springs were also used, although townspeople generally understood that water downstream of tanneries, butchers, and latrines was unfit to drink. Many households collected rainwater in barrels or cisterns.

Wealthier towns invested in piped supplies. In the thirteenth century, London built the Great Conduit, which carried spring water from Tyburn through lead pipes to a public cistern in Cheapside. Siena dug miles of underground tunnels, the bottini, to feed its fountains, and monasteries often possessed the most sophisticated systems of all.

Professional water carriers sold water door to door, and municipal authorities issued ordinances against fouling wells and watercourses. Contrary to popular belief, medieval people drank water routinely; ale was not simply a safer substitute.

Speaker verification performance degrades substantially when test utterances are short, as i-vectors extracted from limited speech exhibit high variability and reduced reliability. This paper proposes a method for transforming short-utterance i-vectors into representations that more closely resemble those extracted from long utterances, using a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN). The generator is conditioned on the short-utterance i-vector and trained to produce a corresponding long-utterance i-vector, while the discriminator learns to distinguish generated vectors from genuine ones. To preserve speaker identity, the adversarial objective is combined with a reconstruction loss and a speaker-discriminative constraint. Experiments on the NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluation corpus with test segments of varying durations show that the transformed i-vectors consistently reduce equal error rates relative to conventional PLDA baselines, with the largest gains observed for the shortest utterances.

We study a class of semi-linear elliptic boundary value problems in which the nonlinear production term is multiplied by a spatially varying scaling coefficient, a structure that arises in models of reaction–diffusion, population dynamics and heat generation. Since such problems generally cannot be solved in closed form and standard Newton-type schemes require costly Jacobian evaluations, we propose a linearization method that replaces the nonlinear problem with a sequence of linear elliptic problems. Each iterate is obtained by solving a linear equation whose coefficients depend only on the previous approximation, with a stabilization parameter chosen from the Lipschitz constant of the nonlinearity. Under suitable assumptions on the scaling function and the source, we prove that the iterative sequence is well defined and converges strongly in H¹ to the unique weak solution, and we derive an a priori error estimate showing geometric convergence. Numerical experiments based on a finite element discretization confirm the theoretical findings and illustrate the efficiency of the approach.

What you're describing is incredibly common, and it has less to do with not understanding sleep and more to do with how your brain weighs the present against the future.

**1. "Revenge bedtime procrastination"**
If your days feel packed with obligations (work, school, family, other people's needs), the late-night hours may be the only time that feels truly yours. Staying up becomes a way of reclaiming freedom, even when you're not doing anything particularly enjoyable. Going to bed feels like handing the day back to responsibilities.

**2. The costs are delayed, the rewards are immediate**
Watching one more episode or scrolling a bit longer pays off right now. Being tired is a problem for "tomorrow you," who feels like a slightly different, more abstract person. Knowing something is bad for you rarely beats a reward that's sitting in your hand.

**3. Fatigue weakens self-control**
The later it gets, the more tired you are, and the harder it is to make disciplined decisions. Ironically, the moment you most need willpower to put the phone down is when you have the least of it.

**4. Screens are designed to keep you there**
Autoplay, infinite feeds and notifications remove natural stopping points. There's never a moment where the content says "that's enough."

**5. Your body clock may be shifted**
Some people genuinely have a later chronotype, meaning they don't feel sleepy until late. Bright screens in the evening can push that clock even later.

**6. Avoidance**
Sometimes bedtime is when worries show up. Staying busy keeps anxious thoughts at bay.

**What tends to help**
- Give yourself real leisure time earlier in the evening so the night doesn't have to compensate.
- Set a "wind-down" alarm 30–60 minutes before bed, not just a wake-up alarm.
- Charge your phone outside the bedroom, or at least across the room.
- Make the bedtime routine pleasant (a book, a shower, music) so it's something you move toward rather than give up for.
- Keep a consistent wake time, even on weekends; it pulls your bedtime earlier over time.

If the pattern persists despite changes, or you lie awake unable to sleep, it may be worth talking to a doctor about insomnia or a circadian rhythm issue.

On my first day in office, I signed an executive order requiring every federal employee to take a forty-minute nap at 2 p.m.

I should explain. I won the presidency by accident: a write-in campaign that started as a joke on a bass-fishing forum, and by the time anyone took it seriously, I'd carried thirty-one states. Four days into the job, I learned that the president gets briefed at 6:30 every morning and that nobody would let me cancel. I wanted out. Impeachment seemed like the fastest exit.

Nap Time lasted two weeks before the Department of Labor reported that federal productivity had jumped eighteen percent. Workplace accidents dropped. Half the Fortune 500 adopted the policy voluntarily. My approval rating rose nine points.

Fine. I escalated.

I listed Air Force One on an online auction site with the description "big plane, runs great, some missiles removed." It sold for 1.3 billion dollars to a tech billionaire who also agreed to cover its maintenance. Economists called it the most efficient asset sale in American history. Cable news ran a segment titled "Is He a Genius?"

I was getting desperate. I skipped the State of the Union and instead livestreamed myself reading every bill Congress had sent me, word for word, in a monotone, pausing whenever I hit something I didn't understand. It took eleven hours. Sixty million people watched. Three senators resigned after I reached page 840 of the farm bill and asked, out loud, why there was a subsidy for a golf course.

For my final attempt, I sent my mother to negotiate a trade deal with China. She had no diplomatic experience. She did have forty years of running the church bake sale. She came home with tariff reductions, a panda loan, and the premier's recipe for scallion pancakes, which she has since improved.

Last week, the House Judiciary Committee finally convened to discuss me. I watched from the Oval Office couch, full of hope.

They voted unanimously to propose a constitutional amendment allowing me a third term.

I'm going to take a nap.

**Nigerians Vote in Tight Presidential Race Amid Fears Over Disputed Result**

LAGOS, Nigeria — Millions of Nigerians lined up at polling stations on Saturday to choose between incumbent President Goodluck Jonathan and former military ruler Muhammadu Buhari, in what analysts say could be the most closely fought election since the country returned to civilian rule in 1999.

The vote pits Jonathan, of the long-dominant People's Democratic Party (PDP), against Buhari, a retired major general who leads the All Progressives Congress (APC), a coalition of opposition parties formed in 2013. It is the first time since the end of military rule that an opposition candidate has been widely seen as having a realistic chance of unseating a sitting president.

Voting got off to a slow start in many areas as electoral officials struggled with new biometric card readers intended to curb fraud. Jonathan himself could not be verified by a card reader at his polling unit in his home state of Bayelsa and had to be accredited manually. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) extended voting into Sunday in some places hit by technical problems.

The election was originally scheduled for Feb. 14 but was pushed back six weeks after security chiefs said they could not guarantee safety in the northeast, where the Islamist militant group Boko Haram has waged a six-year insurgency that has killed thousands and displaced more than a million people.

Security has dominated the campaign. Buhari, who led Nigeria briefly in the 1980s after a coup, has presented himself as a disciplined leader capable of defeating the insurgents and rooting out corruption. Jonathan's supporters point to recent military gains against Boko Haram and to economic growth during his tenure, though falling oil prices have squeezed government revenues and weakened the naira.

The race also reflects Nigeria's long-standing regional and religious divides. Buhari, a Muslim, draws much of his support from the predominantly Muslim north, while Jonathan, a Christian, is strongest in the south, including the oil-producing Niger Delta.

Those divisions have fueled concern that the losing side may refuse to accept the result. After the 2011 election, in which Jonathan defeated Buhari, rioting in parts of the north left around 800 people dead, according to Human Rights Watch.

In January, both candidates signed an accord in Abuja pledging to campaign peacefully and respect the outcome, but tensions have remained high. Some militants in the Niger Delta have warned of unrest if Jonathan loses, while some Buhari supporters have vowed to resist any result they consider rigged.

International observers, including teams from the African Union and the European Union, are monitoring the vote, and world leaders have urged Nigerians to keep the process peaceful.

INEC chairman Attahiru Jega has said results will be collated at the state level before being announced in Abuja, with official figures expected in the coming days.

To win outright, a candidate needs a simple majority of votes nationwide and at least 25 percent of the vote in two-thirds of Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

Subject: Concern about EBS

Hi [Name],

While reviewing our AWS account last week, I came across several issues with how we're using EBS (Elastic Block Store). None of them is an emergency on its own, but together they add up to unnecessary cost and a real security risk, so I wanted to raise them before our next infrastructure review.

**Unattached volumes.** We have [number] volumes sitting in the "available" state, meaning they aren't attached to any instance. Most look like leftovers from instances terminated during last quarter's migration. We're still paying for all of that storage, roughly [$X] per month.

**Unencrypted volumes.** Several production volumes, including some attached to our database servers, don't have encryption at rest enabled. That conflicts with our data-handling policy and would almost certainly be flagged in an audit.

**Snapshot sprawl.** There's no lifecycle policy on our snapshots, and some go back more than two years. A number of them belong to volumes that no longer exist.

**Outdated volume types.** Most of our volumes are still gp2. Moving to gp3 would cut storage costs by about 20% per GB and let us provision performance independently of volume size. The change can be made in place, without downtime.

**The Wall at Okafor's**

Every Sunday morning, the brick wall beside Okafor's Laundromat filled up with stories.

Nobody could say exactly how it started. One week there was a single index card thumbtacked to the corkboard by the door, six lines about a cat who believed she was a lighthouse. The next Sunday there were eleven cards. By the end of that summer the board had spread across the whole side of the building, and people walked over from three neighborhoods just to read it.

The only rule was painted on a strip of plywood at the top: LEAVE A STORY, LEAVE A COMMENT.

Comments went on sticky notes beneath each card. Most were kind. *Loved the ending. Who is the woman in the blue coat? Please write more about the cat.*

Some were not kind, and that was where Mrs. Okafor came in.

She had run the laundromat for thirty-one years. Every Sunday evening she walked the length of the wall with a coffee can, removing the cruel notes, the advertisements, and the cards that were really just phone numbers. She re-pinned whatever the wind had loosened. When rain was forecast, she covered the board with a plastic tarp. She never wrote anything herself.

Theo had been leaving stories since April, always unsigned, always on green cards so he could find them again. He was fifteen and had never told anyone he wrote. He read every comment on his cards twice, once quickly and once slowly.

In October, a new card appeared at the top of the wall in Mrs. Okafor's careful block capitals.

MY KNEES ARE GETTING OLD AND THE WALL IS GETTING BIG. I NEED HELP KEEPING IT. IF YOU LOVE THIS PLACE, COME INSIDE AND ASK.

Within a day, sticky notes crowded beneath it. *We love you, Mrs. O! Thank you for everything. Someone should totally do this.*

Nobody came inside.

Theo stood in front of the card for a long time that Sunday. Then he took a green index card from his pocket, wrote three words, and pinned it beneath hers.

*I'll do it.*

When he pushed open the door, the dryers were humming, and Mrs. Okafor was already holding out a second coffee can.

"How did you know it was me?" he asked.

"Who do you think," she said, "has been keeping the rain off your stories since April?"

**Indonesia Executes Eight Drug Convicts Despite International Appeals**

JAKARTA — Indonesia executed eight death row prisoners early Wednesday, including two Australians and a Brazilian, drawing sharp condemnation from foreign governments that had spent months pleading for clemency.

The prisoners were shot by firing squad shortly after midnight on Nusa Kambangan, a high-security prison island off the southern coast of Java. All eight had been convicted of drug trafficking offenses.

Among those killed were Australians Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, ringleaders of the so-called "Bali Nine," a group arrested in 2005 for attempting to smuggle heroin out of Indonesia. Brazilian Rodrigo Gularte, who was arrested in 2004 for attempting to bring cocaine into the country hidden in surfboards, was also executed, along with four Nigerian men and one Indonesian.

A ninth prisoner, Mary Jane Veloso of the Philippines, received a last-minute reprieve after a woman suspected of recruiting her as a drug courier surrendered to police in the Philippines. Her supporters had argued that she was an unwitting victim of human trafficking.

**Brazil expresses 'deepest sympathy'**

Brazil's government said it had received the news "with deep consternation" and extended its "deepest sympathy" to Gularte's family. Brazilian officials had repeatedly asked Indonesia to spare Gularte, arguing that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and should not be executed because of his mental illness.

It was the second execution of a Brazilian citizen in Indonesia this year. In January, Marco Archer Cardoso Moreira was executed for drug smuggling, prompting President Dilma Rousseff to recall Brazil's ambassador from Jakarta. Relations between the two countries have since been strained, and Rousseff had earlier delayed accepting the credentials of Indonesia's new ambassador to Brazil.

**Australia condemns 'cruel and unnecessary' executions**

Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott described the executions as "cruel and unnecessary," noting that both Chan and Sukumaran had been "fully rehabilitated" during their decade in prison. Chan had become a pastor, and Sukumaran an accomplished painter who taught art classes to fellow inmates.

"We respect Indonesia's sovereignty, but we do deplore what's been done," Abbott told reporters in Canberra, announcing that Australia would withdraw its ambassador for consultations. It is the first time Australia has recalled an ambassador from Indonesia over an execution.

The families of the two men had kept a vigil on the island in the days before the executions and made emotional public appeals to Indonesian President Joko Widodo.

**Widodo stands firm**

Widodo, who took office in October, has refused all requests for clemency in drug cases, arguing that Indonesia faces a narcotics "emergency" that kills dozens of young people every day. His government has said that foreign pressure will not influence the country's legal process, and officials have rejected suggestions that the executions were politically motivated.

The executions also drew criticism from the United Nations and human rights groups, which argue that the death penalty is not an effective deterrent to drug crime and that drug offenses do not meet the threshold of "most serious crimes" under international law. Amnesty International called the executions "utterly reprehensible."

Indonesia resumed executions in 2013 after a four-year pause. With dozens more prisoners still on death row for drug offenses, officials have indicated that further executions are likely.
